tapeLine: Wednesday's post-Fed selloff fully reversed Thursday: the S&P 500 rose 1.1% to 7,637.76, the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.7% to 26,418.30 and the Dow added 316.14 points (+0.6%) to 51,778.04, per the AP's Thursday market wrap, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.93% from Wednesday's Fed-day close near 5.02%. Thursday's US data leaned firm rather than soft: initial jobless claims fell 10,000 to 196,000 for the week of 12 September, the lowest since July, and the Philadelphia Fed's September manufacturing index cooled to 37.8 from August's 47.4 but still beat the 30.5 consensus, per RTTNews. Housing was mixed — total starts fell 2.6% to a 1.275 million annualized rate as multifamily construction dropped, even as single-family starts jumped 7.6% to 918,000 and permits slipped 1.8% — and NAR's pending home sales index rose 0.3% in August but stayed 4.7% below a year ago. Overnight, the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% from 1.0% in a split vote, a 31-year high, and Asian equities rallied on Wall Street's rebound and easing oil: the Nikkei 225 gained 1.9% to 65,332.57 and the Kospi jumped 2.3% to 6,866.83, per AP's Friday wrap. Brent extended its slide toward $102.57 Friday morning as traders weighed fresh Houthi strikes on Saudi targets against signs more Saudi crude could reach the market despite them, per CNBC. Today is a quadruple-witching Friday — stock-index futures, index options, stock options and single-stock futures all expire — a distinct source of late-session volume and volatility. Industrial production/capacity utilization (9:15 ET) and the Conference Board's Leading Economic Index (10:00 ET) are the day's scheduled US data.
matters:
Thursday undid Wednesday's Fed-day selloff: the S&P 500 rose 1.1% to 7,637.76, the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.7% to 26,418.30 and the Dow added 316.14 points (0.6%) to 51,778.04, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased back to 4.93% from Wednesday's Fed-day close near 5.02%, per the AP's Thursday market wrap. Falling oil prices and the retreat in yields did the work — not a change in the Fed outlook itself, which still points to one more 2026 hike per Wednesday's dot plot.

The first US data since the FOMC blackout lifted argued against, not for, an early unwind of that second hike. Initial jobless claims fell 10,000 to 196,000 for the week of 12 September, the lowest since July, with continuing claims at a more-than-two-year low, per Bloomberg. The Philadelphia Fed's September manufacturing index cooled to 37.8 from August's 47.4 but still beat the 30.5 consensus, per RTTNews. Housing was the exception that muddies the picture: total starts fell 2.6% to a 1.275 million annualized rate on a multifamily pullback, even as single-family starts jumped 7.6% to 918,000; single-family permits slipped 1.8%; and NAR's pending home sales index rose only 0.3% in August and remained 4.7% below a year earlier, per NAR's Thursday release. Labor data firmed the hike case; housing stayed soft. The dot plot's extra 2026 hike is still a call on data that hasn't fully arrived.

Overnight, the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% from 1.0% in a split vote — a 31-year high — and Asian equities rallied on Wall Street's rebound and easing oil prices: the Nikkei 225 gained 1.9% to 65,332.57, the Kospi jumped 2.3% to 6,866.83 and Hong Kong's Hang Seng added roughly 0.7%, per AP's Friday wrap.

The oil-pipeline story this brief has tracked since 10 September now runs alongside a second, distinct threat: Yemen's Houthi rebels have pushed south along the Red Sea coast and struck Saudi targets over the past week, reigniting Yemen's civil war and threatening a maritime chokepoint separate from the East-West pipeline itself, per ABC News (Australia) and NPR. Brent nonetheless extended its slide to about $102.57 Friday morning — a third straight losing session — as traders weighed the fresh Houthi strikes against signs more Saudi crude could still reach the market, per CNBC. The pipeline's own repair timeline (half capacity within days, full capacity in roughly six weeks per Bloomberg's Wednesday reporting) is unchanged, but it is no longer the only supply risk in this thread.

The AI-China story stayed on its separate, political track. Preparations for a bilateral AI risk-and-safety dialogue ahead of the 24 September Trump-Xi summit in Washington are reportedly underway, though timing, participants and agenda remain unsettled, per Nikkei Asia; the summit's broader agenda also covers trade, semiconductors, rare earths and Taiwan. No crossover into the rate story has emerged.

The financing thread stayed open for a fifth session: no new debt-financed sponsor buyout has printed since Sequence Holdings/DFO's mostly-equity purchase of Baldwin Group on 14 September, and Friday's search turned up no new candidate.

Invalidation: today is a quadruple-witching Friday, when index and single-stock futures and options all expire together; volume and price swings into the close can run well ahead of anything in the news, so late-session moves should be read with that in mind rather than as fresh signal. Weekend risk around the Houthi-Saudi confrontation is also live and untested by this brief.
alsoOnTape: Today is a quadruple-witching Friday — stock-index futures, index options, stock options and single-stock futures all expire simultaneously — historically a source of elevated volume and late-session volatility independent of news flow. With the FOMC blackout lifted, Fed officials are free to speak on the record again on the pipeline dispute, the AI-China story or the financing test; none had done so as of this writing.

regime.tag: Post-hike rally intact; Houthi supply risk layered onto the pipeline story; financing test still open
regime.sizing: Thursday's rally reversed Wednesday's Fed-day selloff on falling oil and easing yields, not on any change to the Fed's own signal of one more 2026 hike. The first post-blackout data leaned toward reinforcing that second hike (firm claims, a Philly Fed beat) rather than undermining it, while housing stayed soft, so the dot plot's extra hike remains unconfirmed either way. The oil thread has gained a second, distinct risk in the Houthi advance along the Red Sea, layered on top of the East-West pipeline repair already in progress. The financing test set on 10 September remains open with no new candidate. Today is quadruple-witching, which can exaggerate late-session price action independent of any of the above.

secondOrder: Five threads carried into Friday. The Fed-data thread got its first real test: Thursday's jobless claims and Philly Fed both came in firm-to-beat, which argues for follow-through on the dot plot's second 2026 hike rather than against it, while housing starts and pending home sales stayed soft — leaving the hike call genuinely undecided rather than resolved. The oil thread split into two: the East-West pipeline's own repair timeline (six weeks to full capacity) is unchanged, but Houthi attacks along the Red Sea coast have added a second, geographically distinct supply risk that this brief had not previously tracked, even as Friday's price action (Brent's third straight down day) suggests the market is for now pricing more supply, not less. The AI-China thread stayed detached from markets but gained texture: a bilateral AI risk dialogue is reportedly being prepared ahead of the 24 September Trump-Xi summit, though its shape is still unsettled. The financing thread stayed open for a fifth session with no new debt-financed buyout since Baldwin on 14 September. And a new, mechanical thread opened today: quadruple witching, which can move prices on its own independent of any of the fundamental threads above.

scorecard.text: The 17 September brief's tapeLine cited futures pointing to a Thursday recovery of roughly Dow +0.7%, S&P 500 +0.8%, Nasdaq-100 +1.1%. The actual session beat that indication: the S&P 500 rose 1.1% to 7,637.76, the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.7% to 26,418.30 and the Dow added 0.6% to 51,778.04, per the AP's Thursday close.

The 17 September brief flagged that a soft initial-claims or housing print Thursday would move the odds priced for the dot plot's second 2026 hike. The actual data was split: claims fell to a two-month low and the Philly Fed beat consensus (arguing for the hike), while housing starts and pending home sales stayed soft (arguing against it). The second-hike call remains genuinely unresolved.

The financing test set on 10 September — a large, freshly debt-financed sponsor buyout printing — is still open. No new candidate has surfaced since Sequence Holdings/DFO's Baldwin Group deal on 14 September, and Friday's research turned up nothing new.

The 15-17 September briefs treated the Amodei/China AI-slowdown dispute as running on a track separate from Fed policy. That held again Friday: reporting on preparations for a bilateral AI risk-and-safety dialogue ahead of the 24 September Trump-Xi summit showed no crossover into the rate or markets story.
